_meta.source: toy experiment trained for this explainer (src/text_prep.py, src/text_ebt.py, src/text_eval.py)
_meta.note: Toy model trained for this explainer, NOT a paper result. Character-level (54 symbols), ~0.27M params, a few minutes on 1 CPU thread. Loss in nats per character; perplexity is per character (not comparable to the paper's per-token perplexities).
_meta.verified: Energies, gradients, example traces, energy slices and the held-out thinking curve were recomputed independently in plain numpy from the exported weights (src/text_verify.py).

takeaways: Toy model trained for this explainer, not a paper result. All numbers are nats per character on held-out text.

Same-size feed-forward baseline beats the toy EBT by a wide margin: held-out loss 1.599 vs 2.331 at N=3 (per-char perplexity 4.95 vs 10.29), after the same 8000 optimizer steps (EBT 483 s vs baseline 173 s wall-clock).

Thinking longer helps the toy EBT in-distribution: N=3 -> 16 lowers held-out loss 2.331 -> 2.250 (7.8% lower perplexity; paired 95% CI of the gain 0.063 to 0.093 nats). It never closes the gap to the baseline.

The thinking gain shrinks as the data shift grows (opposite of the paper's Fig 7 trend). Perplexity change from N=3 to N=16: 7.8% lower on RedPajama held-out, 5.4% lower on Shakespeare, 3.5% HIGHER on Python code (code improves only 1.0% up to N=5, then gets worse).

Self-verification works without any external verifier: picking the lowest-energy of M=8 candidates (N=3) gives held-out loss 2.250 vs 2.329 for a single candidate (7.6% lower perplexity), while the average candidate stays at 2.330. An oracle that knows the answer would reach 1.869, so energy is a useful but imperfect verifier.

Energy as uncertainty is weak in this toy: across held-out characters, final energy correlates with loss at Spearman 0.29 (prediction entropy: 0.58). Raw energy does NOT separate easy from hard characters the way the paper's Fig 8 does (easy -3.97 vs hard -4.07 mean final energy); only the per-context relative energy E - E(uniform) does (easy -3.18 vs hard -2.91).

Example traces are single random starts. The exported 'q is almost always followed by u' trace first settles on 'r' and only reaches 'u' at step 6; over 256 other starts 'u' is already the top guess at N=3 in 99% of cases. Show it as one start that needed more thinking, not as typical behaviour.

arch.encoder: concat 40x12 char embeddings -> Linear(480,192) -> SiLU -> Linear(192,128) = h
arch.ebt: p = softmax(yhat) (yhat in R^54 are logits); e = p @ Wpe (54x128); z = [h, e, h*e] (384); E = Linear(224,1)(SiLU(Linear(224,224)(SiLU(Linear(384,224)(z))))) -> scalar
arch.baseline: same encoder; logits = Linear(300,54)(SiLU(Linear(300,300)(SiLU(Linear(128,300)(h))))) in one forward pass
arch.linear: y = x @ W + b with W shaped [in, out]
arch.thinking: yhat_{i+1} = yhat_i - alpha * dE/dyhat (yhat_i), yhat_0 ~ N(0, I)

hparams.alpha_sampling: per sample: alpha0 * exp(U(-ln f, ln f)), f = alpha_random_factor
hparams.langevin_note: noise added on every thinking step except the last
hparams.replay_note: a quarter of each batch restarts from the stored final prediction of an earlier batch for the same context (simulates longer thinking trajectories, Sec 3.3)
hparams.loss: cross-entropy(softmax(yhat_N), next char), last step only, backprop through all steps (second-order grads)

train_curves.note: ebt train_loss_ema includes Langevin noise, random alpha/N and replay; train_eval/val use deterministic thinking with alpha0 and N=3. Baseline: one forward pass.

thinking_curve.bon_note: Best-of-M results live in the top-level 'bon' key

bon.note: M candidates from different random yhat_0 ~ N(0,I), fixed alpha, N steps, no noise; keep the candidate with the lowest final energy (no external verifier). 'oracle' picks the candidate with the lowest true loss (upper bound, uses the answer); 'mean' is the average candidate.

uncertainty.rule: easy = 'u' after 'q' or 3rd+ letter inside a word; hard = first letter of a new word; other = everything else. All positions start from the same yhat_0. rel_energy = E(x, yhat_i) - E(x, uniform guess yhat=0): our per-context normalization (removes each context's energy offset), not something the paper defines.
uncertainty.caveat: Raw mean final energy is LOWER for hard characters than for easy ones in this toy (-4.066 vs -3.965), so a raw-energy easy/hard plot would contradict the paper's Fig 8 pattern. Show rel_energy only with its definition, and label it as our normalization.

energy_vs_loss.note: across 4096 held-out positions, after 8 thinking steps (same yhat_0 for all). Positive energy-vs-loss correlation would mean higher energy = harder/less certain.
